title: JUnit 5 & Mockito: test behaviour, fake the boundary
summary: The JUnit 5 test lifecycle and assertions, testing behaviour through the public API, Mockito stubs, default answers, argument matching and verification, spies, why to fake your own boundary instead of mocking types you do not own, and what makes a fake trustworthy.

quiz.prompt: A JUnit 5 test class has the field `List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>()`. Test A adds an item; test B asserts that `seen` is empty. What happens when both run?
choices: B fails whenever A happens to run first
B fails, because JUnit runs the methods in declaration order
B passes: each test method gets a new instance of the class
It depends on whether a @BeforeEach method clears the list
quiz.explanation: The default per-method lifecycle builds a fresh test instance for every test method, so instance fields never carry state between tests.

quiz.prompt: What does `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> calc.price("SKU-1", -1))` give the test?
choices: A boolean saying whether the exception was thrown or not
The thrown exception, so its message can be checked too
Nothing; it only prints the exception's stack trace to the console
The message string, or null when nothing was thrown
quiz.explanation: assertThrows fails the test when no exception (or another type) is thrown, and returns the exception otherwise, ready for assertions on its message.

quiz.prompt: `List<Order> findOpen()` on a Mockito mock was never stubbed. What does a call return?
choices: null, like every other unstubbed method
It throws UnsupportedOperationException
A list that holds one mock Order
An empty list, not null
quiz.explanation: Mockito's default answer returns empty collections for collection types, Optional.empty() for Optional, 0 or false for primitives and wrappers, and null for other objects.

quiz.prompt: The test stubs `when(repo.findByEmail("ana@x.io")).thenReturn(Optional.of(ana))`. The code calls `repo.findByEmail("ANA@x.io")`. What does it get?
choices: Optional.empty(): the arguments are matched with equals
Optional.of(ana), because stubs ignore letter case
An exception, since the call matches no stub
null, because the stub has no default value
quiz.explanation: Arguments are compared with equals, and "ANA@x.io" is not equal to "ana@x.io", so the call gets the default answer for an Optional return type.

quiz.prompt: Which dependency is the best candidate for a Mockito mock or a hand-written fake?
choices: A JDBC ResultSet, so that the test needs no database at all
Your own PaymentGateway interface around the card provider
The BigDecimal arithmetic inside the price calculator
The JPA EntityManager that the repository calls into
quiz.explanation: Fake the boundary you own. Third-party types like ResultSet and EntityManager should be tested against the real thing, and plain arithmetic needs no double at all.

quiz.prompt: Why is mocking `EntityManager` in a repository test risky?
choices: Mockito cannot mock interfaces that come from the jakarta packages
Its methods are final, so every stub is silently ignored by Mockito
It encodes your guess of JPA, and a wrong guess still passes
The test would need a whole running Spring context
quiz.explanation: A mock of a type you do not own tests your assumptions about it. A repository test against a real database finds the query, mapping and flush problems the mock hides.

quiz.prompt: A test stubs five methods, calls the service, then verifies all five calls in order. What is the main problem?
choices: verify has no way to check the order in which calls happened
Five stubs make Mockito noticeably slower on every run
It mirrors the implementation, so every refactor breaks it
A stubbed method can no longer be verified
quiz.explanation: The test restates how the service works instead of what it promises. Assert on the outcome, and verify only interactions that are the behaviour.

quiz.prompt: A test writes `when(spy.loadAll()).thenReturn(List.of())` on a spy whose real `loadAll` calls the network. What happens?
choices: The stub takes effect and nothing real runs at any point
The real loadAll runs once while the stub is set up
Mockito refuses, because a spy can never be stubbed at all
The spy turns into a plain mock for every one of its methods
quiz.explanation: when(spy.loadAll()) has to call spy.loadAll() to know what to stub, and on a spy that is the real method. doReturn(...).when(spy).loadAll() stubs without calling it.

quiz.prompt: Many tests will share a payment fake. Which behaviour should it keep from the real gateway?
choices: None: a fake should simply approve every charge it gets
A random delay on every call, so tests feel realistic
A reused idempotency key returns the first charge
A console log line for every call, to help debugging
quiz.explanation: The fake must keep the rules the code relies on. Idempotency is what makes a retry after a timeout safe, so a fake without it cannot test that retry.

quiz.prompt: With `MockitoExtension`'s strict stubs, a test stubs a method that the code under test never calls. What happens?
choices: The test fails with an unnecessary-stubbing error
Nothing at all: unused stubs are simply ignored
The stub carries over into the next test method
Mockito logs a warning and the test passes
quiz.explanation: Strict stubs report a stub nobody used, because it usually means the test or the code is not doing what the author thinks.

flashcards.back: By default a new instance of the test class is created for every test method, so instance fields start fresh in each test.
@BeforeEach runs before every test method; @BeforeAll runs once for the class and is a static method by default.
Unstubbed calls return null for most objects, zero or false for primitives and wrappers, and empty collections, Optional or streams for those types.

flashcards.front: How does Mockito match a stub's arguments?
flashcards.back: With equals on each argument, unless matchers are used, and then every argument of that call must be a matcher.
Stub to supply the inputs a test needs; verify only the interactions that are themselves the behaviour, such as one receipt email.

flashcards.front: Don't mock what you don't own
flashcards.back: Mock or fake your own interfaces at the boundary, and test third-party types such as JDBC or JPA against the real thing.
Use doReturn(value).when(spy).method(), because when(spy.method()) runs the real method while setting up the stub.
It keeps the real dependency's rules, such as idempotency keys and declines, so tests fail where production would fail.

drills.title: A payment fake that keeps the gateway's rules
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Checkout retries a charge once when the gateway times out. Prove it never charges a customer twice, without calling the real provider."

**Why it matters.** A gateway can time out AFTER it charged the card: the money moved, only the response was lost. The retry is safe only because it reuses the idempotency key. A fake that approves everything, or fails before charging, cannot show that; a fake that keeps the real rules can.

**Your task.** Complete `FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway`:
- `charge(key, card, cents)` with `cents <= 0` throws `IllegalArgumentException` ("amount must be positive") and records nothing
- a key seen before returns the FIRST charge made with it, without charging again
- otherwise make a new charge with the next id (`ch_1`, `ch_2`, ...): `DECLINED` when the card is in `declinedCards`, else `APPROVED`
- after `loseNextResponse()`, the next NEW charge is made and recorded as usual, but the call throws `GatewayTimeout` instead of returning it (only that one call)
- `charges()` returns a snapshot of every charge made, in order: charging later must not change a list handed out earlier

`Checkout` (given) is the code under test.

**Worked example.** `loseNextResponse()`, then `checkout.pay("7", "card-1", 1200)`: the first call charges `ch_1` and throws, the retry with key `order-7` gets `ch_1` back, and `charges()` holds one charge.
hints: The rules worth keeping are the ones the retry depends on: what happens to a repeated key, and what a timeout after charging leaves behind.

Refuse bad amounts before anything else, answer a known key with its stored charge, and otherwise build the next charge, store it under its key and in the history, and only then decide whether this call loses its response. Hand out copies of the history.

Keep a map from key to charge and a list of every charge, replay known keys, record new charges before any simulated timeout, reset the lost-response flag once it fires, and copy the list when asked for it.

drills.title: Build the mock Mockito builds
drills.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "What does `mock(OrderRepo.class)` actually return, and why does an unstubbed `findOpen()` give an empty list instead of null? Build a small one."

**Why it matters.** A Mockito mock is a proxy that records every call, answers stubbed calls whose arguments are `equals` to the stub's, and gives every other call a default answer: empty collections and `Optional.empty()`, zero and false for primitives AND their wrappers, `null` for other objects. Knowing those rules explains most "why did my mock return that?" surprises.

**Your task.** Complete `Mock<T>` (a JDK `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` over the interface):
- `static <T> Mock<T> of(Class<T> type)` and `T object()`, the proxy itself
- `when(String method, List<Object> args, Object result)` stubs one call; stubbing the same method and arguments again replaces the result (the last stubbing wins). A no-argument call has `args` = `List.of()`
- every call through the proxy is recorded; a stubbed call returns its result; any other call returns the default for the method's return type:
  - `List`/`Collection` an empty list, `Set` an empty set, `Map` an empty map, `Optional` `Optional.empty()`
  - `boolean`/`Boolean` false; `int`, `long`, `short`, `byte` and their wrappers 0 of that type; `double`/`float` and wrappers 0.0; `char` `'\0'`
  - anything else (including `void` and `String`) `null`
- `int calls(String method, List<Object> args)`: how many recorded calls had that method name and `equals` arguments
- the `Object` methods are not recorded: `toString()` returns `"Mock for " + simple interface name`, `equals` is identity, `hashCode` is `System.identityHashCode(proxy)`

**Worked example.** After `m.when("findByEmail", List.of("ana@x.io"), Optional.of("Ana"))`, `m.object().findByEmail("ANA@x.io")` returns `Optional.empty()`.
hints: A proxy sends every call, even toString, to one handler; the mock's whole behaviour is how that handler answers.

Treat the Object methods separately, otherwise record the method name with the argument list, return a stored result when one exists for exactly that name and those arguments, and else pick a default from the method's return type, checking collections and Optional before the primitives and their wrappers.

Keep a map from a name-and-arguments record to the stubbed result and a list of the same records for every call, answer from the map or from a default chosen by the declared result type, and count matching records when asked.
